Chapter 9, Rājavidyārājaguhyayoga, "the royal knowledge, the royal secret," has Kṛṣṇa announce to Arjuna the most confidential teaching of the poem so far: knowledge joined with direct realization, easy to practice and imperishable. He opens with a paradox he spends the first third of the chapter working out — the whole world rests in him, pervaded by his unmanifest form, and yet he is not confined within it, as space contains the wind without being limited by it; nature (prakṛti) acts and unwinds the cosmos through endless cycles of creation and dissolution, but only under his oversight, so that he himself remains untouched, seated as if indifferent, by what it does. The deluded, he says, despise him for the human body he has taken on, missing his true nature as the great lord of beings and clinging instead to a demonic, self-defeating nature of their own, while the great-souled take refuge in his divine nature and worship him with undivided minds. Two dense catalog verses have him identify himself outright with every element of Vedic sacrifice and every name for ultimate reality — the rite, the offering, the fire, the mantra, the Vedas themselves, father, mother, being and non-being — before two four-line verses turn this into a pointed critique of ritualists who win only a temporary heaven and cycle back to mortal life once their merit runs out, unlike those who seek Kṛṣṇa himself and are freed for good. He promises to personally look after the welfare of those exclusively devoted to him, concedes that even worship of other deities, done with faith, ultimately reaches him (if not by the correct method), and lays out the simplest possible devotional practice: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, offered with devotion, accepted from anyone of disciplined mind, with the instruction to turn every action, every meal, every gift and every austerity into an offering to him. The chapter closes on its most radical promise, that even a person of thoroughly wicked conduct becomes a saint through undivided devotion, and that the supreme goal is open equally to women, merchants and laborers, and all the more so to the pious and the royal sages, if only they take refuge in him and make him their highest goal.
